subject: Chemistry
title: ClF₃: The Chemical That Sets Fire to Anything
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on ClF₃: The Chemical That Sets Fire to Anything.

hook.text: Chlorine trifluoride is so reactive it sets fire to glass, sand, asbestos, and even water. It burned through a concrete floor.

buildup.text: ClF₃ is a stronger oxidizer than oxygen itself. It rips electrons from nearly any material it contacts.

discovery.text: In one spill, a ton of ClF₃ burned through 30 cm of concrete and 90 cm of gravel beneath it before stopping.

twist.text: The Nazis tried to use ClF₃ as a weapon called 'N-stoff.' Even they found it too dangerous to handle.

climax.text: Rocket scientist John Clark wrote: 'It can be extinguished with nothing.' No firefighting method works on ClF₃ fires.

punchline.text: It burns concrete, ignites water, and has no extinguisher. Chemistry's angriest molecule.

quiz.question: What makes chlorine trifluoride so extremely dangerous?
options: It's a stronger oxidizer than oxygen and reacts violently with almost any material
It produces invisible toxic fumes that are undetectable
It explodes on contact with any metal surface

details.summary: Chlorine trifluoride is a hypergolic oxidizer so powerful that it can set fire to glass, sand, water, and materials that have already been burned. Developed as a potential rocket fuel and weapon, it is one of the most dangerous chemicals ever produced and is nearly impossible to contain safely.
details.whyItMatters: Chlorine trifluoride represents the extreme edge of chemical reactivity, used as a cautionary example in chemistry education about the limits of safe chemical handling.
takeaways: ClF3 ignites materials that are normally considered fireproof
It was tested as a weapon and rocket propellant during World War II
A one-ton spill burned through concrete and gravel simultaneously

faq.question: How can chlorine trifluoride set fire to things that are already burned?
faq.answer: ClF3 is such a powerful oxidizer that it can fluorinate materials that have already been fully oxidized by oxygen. Ash and rust, which cannot burn further in air, contain elements that fluorine can still strip more electrons from, releasing heat and creating fires.

faq.question: Is chlorine trifluoride used for anything practical today?
faq.answer: Yes, in very small quantities. The semiconductor industry uses ClF3 for cleaning chemical vapor deposition chambers because it aggressively removes residue. It is handled under extremely controlled conditions with specialized equipment designed to resist its extraordinary reactivity.
